tagline: Rolling prairie, creek crossings and a ranch remade as a preserve
intro: K-177 carries the Flint Hills Scenic Byway through rolling tallgrass country between Council Grove and Cassoday. This is a two-lane drive with curves and creek crossings; Kansas Tourism lists the route at 47 miles. Kansas Tourism presents the National Scenic Byway as a way to see native prairie grasses and flowers, while the federal byway profile recommends an hour for the drive.

The highway once carried the number K-13 before becoming K-177. At the byway’s northern end, Council Grove’s Main Street follows the older Santa Fe Trail. Along the modern road, another change came in 1996, when Tallgrass Prairie National Preserve was established to protect a remnant of the grassland. The National Park Service reports that less than 4% of North America’s tallgrass prairie remains intact, mostly in the Kansas Flint Hills.

Heading south from Council Grove, the road passes through the preserve before reaching Strong City and crossing the Cottonwood River into Cottonwood Falls. Farther south, curves lead past Bazaar, with stretches beside the railway on the way to Matfield Green. The byway’s 1680 AM broadcasts explain prairie wildlife and pasture burning, with transmitters in Council Grove, Cottonwood Falls and Cassoday. Stay with K-177 to finish in Cassoday.

moments.title: Council Grove
moments.text: Main Street follows the old Santa Fe Trail, placing an earlier overland route at the northern end of this drive. Travelers once left letters in the Post Office Oak for others heading in the right direction to carry onward. The town’s name recalls an agreement with the Osage Nation allowing wagon trains to pass westward along the trail. A post office was established here in 1855. The present Main Street post office was built in 1938–39, and its mural, Charles B. Rogers’s “Autumn Colors,” dates from 1941. Painted for the New Deal post office mural program, it depicts a Flint Hills farm in autumn.

moments.title: Tallgrass Prairie National Preserve
moments.text: Stephen F. Jones completed his ranch headquarters here in 1881, enclosing cattle with walls and fences as open-range ranching gave way to a different system. His Second Empire ranch house dates from that year. The property later became the Z-Bar Ranch, then part of a preservation effort that paired federal management with private landownership. Senator Nancy Kassebaum brought stakeholders together in 1992 after local objections to a park owned entirely by the National Park Service. Bison arrived from Wind Cave National Park in 2009. Fire and grazing help keep trees from taking over the prairie; the preserve’s work includes both.
moments.notice: The historic ranch house dates from 1881; the barn from 1882.

moments.title: Cottonwood Falls
moments.text: Local limestone gives the Chase County Courthouse its walls, while local walnut supplied its three-story winding staircase. Built in 1873, it remains Kansas’s oldest operating courthouse. Architect John G. Haskell also worked on the Kansas State Capitol. Cottonwood Falls had been designated the temporary county seat when Chase County was organized in 1859. The building’s architecture has been described as Second Empire or French Renaissance Revival. Cottonwood Falls sits south of Strong City, on the south side of the Cottonwood River. Through the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, farms and cattle ranches divided much of the surrounding land.
moments.notice: Look for the courthouse’s local limestone exterior.
